name: Parkinson's Law
description: Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
design_relevance_note: Sometimes invoked in productivity-tool design (e.g. deadline/timer features).
myth_risk_note: Downgraded from moderate 2026-09-07: the specific, narrower time-expansion claim this entry is actually graded against now has real, replicated, artifact-controlled backing. Myth risk remains non-zero only because Parkinson's own more sweeping bureaucratic-growth framing (the satirical original claim) is still commonly conflated with the narrower, now-verified individual-level effect in casual design-practice usage.
prevalence_note: 'Work expands to fill the time available' has mainstream cultural currency well beyond design practice, and is routinely invoked in deadline/scope UX discussions.

findings.description: Subjects given excess time to complete a multi-trial task took longer to finish it than subjects given only the minimum time needed -- an early empirical demonstration of the core Parkinson's-law time-expansion effect, framed by the authors as a goal-setting phenomenon (more time functions like a less-difficult implicit goal). Per src-brannon-hershberger-brock-1999's own methodological review, this study's instructions were "replete with time cues," a possible confound (subjects may have been responding to explicit temporal expectations set by the experimenter rather than a general tendency for work to expand) later addressed and ruled out by Brannon et al.'s 1999 artifact-controlled replications.
findings.effect_size: Not independently confirmed (full text inaccessible; direction of effect confirmed via a reliable secondary peer-reviewed source, magnitude not stated there)
findings.source_title: Parkinson's Law as a goal-setting phenomenon

findings.description: When told that a subsequent, expected block of work has been canceled, people reliably prolong ("dally on") their current task compared to controls who expect no such cancellation -- a direct, individual-level behavioral demonstration of Parkinson's law ("work expands to fill the time available"). The effect replicated across two exact replications and a fourth conceptual replication using different, negatively-toned stimuli and an objective (not self-reported) performance measure, addressing a methodological gap the authors identify in earlier demonstrations (see find-parkinsonslaw-time-cued-task-completion): the effect held even when the earlier studies' explicit time-cuing confound was removed.
findings.effect_size: Directional (experimental vs. control time-on-task, reobtained across 4 studies; no single pooled effect size reported)
findings.source_title: Timeless demonstrations of Parkinson's first law

applications.title: Parkinson's own 1955 illustration: a full day spent on one postcard
applications.description: In the 1955 Economist article that first proposed the law, C. Northcote Parkinson illustrated 'work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion' with the case of an elderly woman with unlimited free time who spends an entire day sending a single postcard to her niece -- an hour finding the postcard, another finding her spectacles, half an hour finding the address, over an hour composing the message, and twenty minutes deciding whether to bring an umbrella to the postbox -- versus a busy person who could dispatch the same task in three minutes total.
applications.ethical_note: A general observation about time and task management with no persuasion, dark-pattern, or user-manipulation dimension -- included purely as the corpus's real-world (if constructed-as-illustration) misapplication example for a heuristic with no rigorous backing of its own, matching this cell's existing entries like the Pareto Principle's NN/g worked example.
